surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (Europe)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership, usage patterns, purchase drivers, and unmet needs.

segments.name: Health-Focused Users
segments.description: Buy a smartwatch primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking (heart rate, sleep, workouts). They use it daily, often wear it to bed, and are willing to pay more for better sensors and battery life. Accuracy is their top concern.

segments.name: Safety-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Purchase smartwatches for themselves or family members (often older parents) for fall detection, emergency SOS, and peace of mind. They value reliability and ease of use over advanced metrics, and are moderately price sensitive.

segments.name: Style-Led Connectors
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch as a fashion accessory and a convenient hub for notifications, calls, and payments. They upgrade frequently to keep up with style and brand trends, and are less concerned with health accuracy. Price is less of a barrier.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Want essential smartwatch functions (notifications, basic activity tracking) at an affordable price. They are highly price sensitive, compare options carefully, and are willing to compromise on advanced features and battery life to stay within budget.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers in Europe. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Europe who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Owns or intends to purchase a smartwatch for personal use within the last 12 months or next 6 months; Primary decision-maker for the purchase; Uses the smartwatch for personal, not employer-mandated, purposes. Excluded: Purchases made by businesses for employee distribution (e.g., corporate wellness programs); Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parental decision); Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model at the point of purchase. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Smartphone users, especially iOS and Android
Value convenience and connectivity (notifications, calls, payments)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.covers: how they shop for and buy it — trigger, research, channel, spend, decision drivers

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how it fits into their daily life — how often it is worn, for what purposes, and who in the household is involved. It then moves into the purchase journey: what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, how much they spent, and which features tipped the decision. Next, it probes deeper into product expectations, forcing trade-offs between battery, accuracy, design, and price to reveal what buyers truly value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and future intent — whether they will upgrade, switch brands, or…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Smartwatches in Europe — who Owns or intends to purchase a smartwatch for personal use within the last 12 months or next 6 months; Primary decision-maker for the purchase; Uses the smartwatch for personal, not employer-mandated, purposes. The audience is defined as individual consumers who buy smartwatches for their own use, reflecting the dominant B2C purchase dynamic. Demographics target adults with disposable income and tech affinity, while qualifiers ensure the respondent is the actual buyer and user.

Uses the smartwatch for personal, not employer-mandated, purposes
behaviors: Smartphone users, especially iOS and Android
Value convenience and connectivity (notifications, calls, payments)
exclusions: Purchases made by businesses for employee distribution (e.g., corporate wellness programs)
Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parental decision)
Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features

contextDemographics.income: Middle to upper-middle income, discretionary spending capacity
contextDemographics.geography: Global, with emphasis on urban and suburban areas

assumptions: The market is primarily consumer-driven, though some enterprise sales exist; these are excluded from the consumer survey.
Smartwatch ownership implies smartphone ownership, which is a prerequisite for full functionality.

questions.question: How long have you owned your current smartwatch?
questions.insight: Top response: Less than 6 months (28.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Health-Focused Users and Style-Led Connectors skew toward recent purchases, while Value-Driven Buyers and Safety-Driven Buyers hold onto devices longer.

questions.question: What do you use your smartwatch for?
questions.insight: Top response: Health and fitness tracking (82.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Health-Focused Users dominate health and sleep tracking; Safety-Driven Buyers lift fall detection; Style-Led Connectors drive style and notifications.

questions.question: How often do you wear your smartwatch?
questions.insight: Top response: Always or almost always (55.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Health-Focused Users and Safety-Driven Buyers wear devices constantly; Style-Led Connectors also high wear; Value-Driven Buyers less frequent.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership, usage patterns, purchase drivers, and unmet needs.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Jobs-to-be-done combined with price sensitivity. The same smartwatch serves fundamentally different needs (health monitoring, safety, style, connectivity), and willingness to pay varies sharply with the job hired. This lens separates buyers more meaningfully than usage frequency alone, which is high

segments.name: Health-Focused Users
segments.description: Buy a smartwatch primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking (heart rate, sleep, workouts). They use it daily, often wear it to bed, and are willing to pay more for better sensors and battery life. Accuracy is their top concern.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high usage frequency, prioritise accuracy and battery life over style, and show moderate-to-low price sensitivity for advanced health features.

segments.name: Safety-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Purchase smartwatches for themselves or family members (often older parents) for fall detection, emergency SOS, and peace of mind. They value reliability and ease of use over advanced metrics, and are moderately price sensitive.
segments.hypothesis: They will cite fall detection and safety features as key purchase drivers, show high interest in family sharing features, and have a longer replacement cycle.

segments.name: Style-Led Connectors
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch as a fashion accessory and a convenient hub for notifications, calls, and payments. They upgrade frequently to keep up with style and brand trends, and are less concerned with health accuracy. Price is less of a barrier.
segments.hypothesis: They will prioritise design and brand over health features, show higher spend on premium models, and replace their watch more often.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Want essential smartwatch functions (notifications, basic activity tracking) at an affordable price. They are highly price sensitive, compare options carefully, and are willing to compromise on advanced features and battery life to stay within budget.
segments.hypothesis: They will report lower spend, prioritise price over premium features, and show higher sensitivity to promotions and entry-level models.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question cp8 (main reason you own a smartwatch) is the most direct behavioural self-report, so if a respondent ties between segments, assign them to the segment matching their stated primary reason.
notes: Only options that clearly discriminate were scored; many options like 'Other' or general usage were left unscored.
Value seekers are identified primarily by price sensitivity and willingness to give up features, as captured in pe6, pe7, pe8, and sf5.
Safety caregivers are identified by explicit mention of fall detection/safety as a reason or must-have.
Style connectors are identified by style/brand as a reason and frequent replacement.
Health optimizers are identified by health/sleep tracking focus and willingness to pay for accuracy.
6 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how it fits into their daily life — how often it is worn, for what purposes, and who in the household is involved. It then moves into the purchase journey: what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, how much they spent, and which features tipped the decision. Next, it probes deeper into product expectations, forcing trade-offs between battery, accuracy, design, and price to reveal what buyers truly value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and future intent — whether they will upgrade, switch brands, or…
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'category relationship' with 'smartwatch ownership and tenure' to capture both current owners and intenders, reflecting the growing market.
Added a beat on 'primary motivation' early to directly capture the jobs-to-be-done lens, which is central to segmenting this category.
In the buying section, added 'research and discovery' as a distinct beat because online reviews and social media heavily influence smartwatch purchases in Europe.
In preferences, added 'compatibility and ecosystem fit' as a category-specific beat because cross-platform issues are a top pain point.
Used a trade-off beat to force choices between battery, accuracy, and price, which is essential for distinguishing value-driven from health-focused buyers.
In satisfaction, included a dedicated 'pain points' beat to capture the top frustrations (battery, accuracy, privacy) that drive switching.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model at the point of purchase. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer, making this a pure B2C market.
